sweep.note: Merged output of eleven separate region sweeps run with the 007-location-sweep skill. Each region was swept individually; per-region scope, sources and open questions are preserved in 'region_sweeps' below. The 'records' array is the single batch for load_to_notion.py.
critical_open_questions: THE LOADER HAS NEVER BEEN DRY-RUN AGAINST ANY OF THIS. All eleven files were built in an environment with no outbound network. Field names and select option values are unconfirmed across all 109 records. Run the dry run before anything else.

Project type, Use case and Concrete opportunity are deliberately left off most records. Only option values actually observed in the live database were used, because inventing a select value fails the write. Let the dry run print the valid lists, then backfill.
AE is unset on 96 of 109 records. Only named-account matches are resolved (7 aled, 4 lisa, 2 avi). Every unset record carries 'AE ROUTING: UNRESOLVED' at the head of Notes rather than a silent guess.

Records whose Name begins 'NO CONTRACTOR IDENTIFIED' or similar are deliberately incomplete and breach the standing rule that every record names a delivery organisation. They are included because each is among the largest projects in its region. None should be presented to a customer or an AE as a priority target until the contractor is resolved.

Cross-region duplicates were actively avoided during the sweeps. Lower Thames Crossing is split (tunnel and Roads North under East of England, Kent Roads under South East). YORbuild 2 is filed once under Yorkshire though it covers the North East and East Midlands. Birmingham's highways framework is filed once under West Midlands though it covers the East Midlands. London Gateway is filed under East of England, not London.

Thinnest coverage, worth a second pass: Wales (4 records against £983m of Q2 2026 awards across 22 projects), South West (Cornwall, Dorset, Wiltshire, Gloucestershire not reached), South East (defence estate at Portsmouth and AWE Aldermaston not searched at all), East of England (Cambridge, Norwich, Herts/Beds not reached), Scotland (the 16-project, £2.7bn utilities cluster only partly captured).

records.body:
## Why it qualifies

Best-timed record in the London sweep. Skanska signed the £282m contract with AshbyCapital on 29 June 2026, Keltbray is finishing demolition, and **construction starts in October 2026** for completion late 2029. Today the frame method, pour sequence and formwork strategy are being set — which is the moment before the decision locks, not after it.

Skanska UK is one of Aled's named accounts, so this is a warm route rather than a cold one.

## Concrete scope

- 23 storeys of repeating commercial office floorplate, c.25,000 sq m
- Retained 1974 basement and lower levels — new structure tying into old substructure, which is where the awkward early-age and differential-movement questions live
- Adjacent 65 Old Broad Street refurbishment and a Grade II-listed Bath House refurbishment running alongside

On a three-year programme with a fixed leasing ambition at the end, floor cycle time is the schedule. That is the clean Cure/Signal argument.

## Entry angle

Go through the existing Skanska UK relationship, not the site. The conversation to have before October is with whoever is setting the frame strategy — the retained-basement interface gives a technical reason to be in the room that a generic monitoring pitch does not.

Secondary angle: Skanska UK has three other live central London office jobs (One Appold Street £273m, South Molton Mayfair £197m, a £105m Baola Properties block). A result here is portable across the account.

## Gaps

No frame subcontractor published. No concrete volumes. No published low-carbon concrete commitment, so do not lead with MixAI here the way you would at One Appold Street.

## Sources

- Skanska UK press release, 29 June 2026
- Construction News, 29 June 2026
- Building, 30 June 2026 (Keltbray demolition, Landsec/AshbyCapital funding structure)

records.body:
## Why it qualifies

A £300m, 36-storey tower at the Old Street/City junction where **main construction works began within weeks of the 10 August 2026 announcement**, running to a 2030 completion. Multiplex was already embedded under a PCSA and has now signed the build contract.

That means roughly four years of frame programme is ahead, and the pour-cycle detail is being worked right now.

## Concrete scope

- 36 repeating commercial floorplates, 475,000 sq ft
- Substructure starting Q3 2026, superstructure to follow
- Central London constrained site at a major junction — logistics pressure makes cycle certainty worth more, not less

On a tower this tall the slab cycle *is* the programme. A day saved per floor is 36 days, and that framing does more selling than any general monitoring pitch.

## Entry angle

Resolve the frame subcontractor first. On a Multiplex London tower the frame is normally let to a specialist, and that specialist — not Multiplex's commercial team — owns pour cycle time and therefore owns the problem Converge solves.

Secondary: Endurance Land has repeat business with Multiplex (Regent Quarter), so a developer-side relationship has legs beyond this scheme.

## Gaps

No frame subcontractor named. No concrete volumes or cycle targets published. No indexed site team yet — contact building will need LinkedIn rather than published sources.

**AE routing is unresolved.** UK is shared, Multiplex is nobody's named account, and the lead product doesn't break the tie.

## Sources

- Construction Enquirer, 10 August 2026

records.body:
## Why it qualifies

£400m, 23 storeys, 450,000 sq ft in the City for Brockton Everlast. Piling began November 2025 and the scheme runs to a Q2 2029 Cat A finish, so the substructure has gone but the tower frame is still largely ahead.

The detail that makes this more than another office tower: the team took a **planning amendment specifically to reduce total emissions and embodied carbon** and to simplify the sub-structural works. Someone on this project is carrying a carbon number they have publicly committed to. That is a mandated commitment, not an aspiration, and it is the strongest MixAI hook in the London sweep.

## Concrete scope

- 23 repeating floorplates at 3.2m net ceiling heights
- Substructure simplified by design amendment — reduced, not eliminated
- Programme deliberately shortened as part of the same amendment, which puts cycle time under stated pressure

## Entry angle

Two doors. The carbon door (MixAI, against a published embodied-carbon reduction the team has already committed to) and the cycle door (Cure/Signal, against a programme they have publicly said they shortened). The second is stronger with Multiplex's commercial team; the first is stronger with AKT II and the developer.

## Gaps

**This record leans on an October 2025 source.** Site status as of August 2026 is not confirmed and should be checked before any approach — if the frame is well advanced the timing score drops. Superstructure frame subcontractor is not published. The embodied carbon target is described qualitatively, never in numbers.

AE routing unresolved: UK shared, no named account.

## Sources

- Construction Enquirer, 16 October 2025

properties.Name: SCS JV (SKANSKA COSTAIN STRABAG) - HS2 Euston Tunnel - London
properties.General contractor/JV: Skanska Costain STRABAG JV (SCS JV) — HS2's London tunnels contractor. Members: Skanska Construction UK, Costain Group plc, STRABAG AG. Segments manufactured by STRABAG at its Hartlepool facility.
properties.Concrete subcontractor: Self-delivered within the JV. STRABAG operates the precast segment factory at Hartlepool; SCL lining works delivered in-house by the JV.
properties.Client: HS2 Ltd (CEO Mark Wild). Euston Partnership Board on the terminus side.
properties.Location: Old Oak Common to Euston, 7.2km twin bore beneath west and central London, 35-50m depth
properties.Competitor present: Not established. HS2 has heavy incumbent instrumentation across the programme — assume something is in place and check before pitching.
properties.Fit reason: 48,294 precast segments across both bores is repeatability at industrial scale, and repeatability is the strongest signal in the mass-concrete profile — a saving on segment curing cycle multiplies 48,000 times. Add SCL lining works at Old Oak Common running through 2026 and cross-passage construction. Access is unusually good: two of the three JV members are named Converge accounts. The reason this is Medium and not High is timing — the TBMs launched in January and March 2026 and reach Euston in 2027, so a large share of the segment production run is already behind, and the Euston terminus itself remains unfunded.
properties.Fit dimensions: Timing: MEDIUM — TBMs launched early 2026, Euston breakthrough 2027; segment casting ongoing but past its midpoint, and the terminus station is unfunded. Opportunity: HIGH — 48,294 segments at 6t each is the most repeatable pour programme in the sweep, plus SCL lining and cross-passages. Access: HIGH — Skanska is Aled's named account, STRABAG is Lisa's; two independent warm routes into the same JV. Coverage: LOW — that same fact is the problem. Skanska and STRABAG sit in different AE territories inside one contracting entity, and this needs deciding rather than assuming.

## Why it qualifies

The Euston Tunnel is a 7.2km twin bore from Old Oak Common to Euston at 35-50m depth, built by Skanska Costain STRABAG. Across both bores **48,294 precast concrete segments** will be installed, each weighing six tonnes, all cast by STRABAG at a purpose-built Hartlepool facility and railed to London.

Repeatability at that scale is the single strongest signal in the mass-concrete profile. A saving on segment curing cycle multiplies 48,000 times.

## Concrete scope

- 48,294 precast segments, 6t each, factory-cast at Hartlepool
- Sprayed concrete lining works at the Old Oak Common end, lining and waterproofing continuing through 2026
- 18 cross-passages still to be constructed

## Why it is Medium, not High

Timing. TBMs Madeleine and Karen launched in January and March 2026 at up to 150m a week and reach Euston in 2027. A meaningful share of the segment run is already cast. And the Euston terminus station itself is still unfunded — the tunnel arrives about 1km short of the proposed station.

Be honest about that rather than selling the programme's headline size. What is actually purchasable in the next year is the remaining segment production and the cross-passage and SCL works, not the whole £bn.

## Entry angle

The Hartlepool segment plant, not the London drives. That is a precast batching conversation about curing cycle and demould strength on a repeating unit, and STRABAG owns it directly.

## Coverage problem — read before acting

Skanska is Aled's named account. STRABAG is Lisa's. They are in the same JV on the same contract. Set to `lisa` here only because STRABAG owns the precast plant where the opportunity sits, but **this needs Lisa and Aled to agree it rather than one of them working it.**

## Gaps

No read on existing instrumentation — HS2 runs heavy incumbent monitoring across the programme and it would be careless to assume a clear field. Contact building deliberately not flagged until routing is settled.

## Sources

- Construction Enquirer, 17 March 2026
- New Civil Engineer, 22 January 2026
- Railway-News, August 2026

## Why it qualifies — and the honest caveat

Old Oak Common is the UK's largest new-build station and the numbers are enormous: an 850m long, 20m deep underground box on about 1,600 reinforced concrete piles, a 45,000 sq m base slab built from 76,000m³ of concrete across **91 separate pours of 600-1,000m³ each**.

All of that is finished. The base slab completed in early 2025 and all six high-speed platforms completed in August 2026. Size is not fit, and it would be misleading to work this record as though the headline pours were ahead.

## What is actually left

HS2's own spring 2026 construction look-ahead lists, running to November 2026:

- Concrete structure works for the HS2 underground station (superstructure above the base slab)
- Concrete frame for the Shared Accommodation Building
- Internal site road and concrete surfaces
- Concrete works and steel to the ventilation shaft and crossover box, plus retaining walls

Real volume. Not the repeatable programme the base slab was.

## Entry angle

**Expanded**, not BBVS. Expanded holds frame, substructure and platform works and owns pour sequence; the JV is a slow and diffuse entry by comparison.

Second angle worth more than it looks: London Concrete (Holcim) runs a **dedicated on-site batching plant** and over 90% of base slab concrete was batched on site. Captive batching plus a BREEAM Outstanding target is a MixAI conversation with a named supplier attached.

## Gaps

No residual concrete volumes published for the remaining scope. No read on existing instrumentation, which on an HS2 station is unlikely to be a clear field. AE routing unresolved.

TfL has named Amey Rail, Costain and Dragados to a £700m framework covering ECI through design, construction and completion across the capital, running 1 June 2026 to 31 May 2028.

records.body:
## Why it qualifies — and why now specifically

The DCO was granted in September 2025, but legal challenges kept the delivery structure frozen. The High Court dismissed them on **23 June 2026**, and the **final challenge was dismissed in early August**.

Gatwick is now moving into **detailed engineering, contractor appointments and enabling works**. The entire £2.2bn delivery structure is being assembled this quarter, and no main contractor exists yet.

That window will not stay open long.

## Read this before any conversation

**This is not a new runway.** It brings the existing northern standby runway into regular use through alterations to the runway, taxiway system and associated infrastructure.

Calling it a second runway build would mark an approach as uninformed immediately. Everyone on the project is precise about this distinction.

## Concrete scope

- Airfield pavement to the runway and taxiway system — thick, high-specification, laid in repeating bays to tight tolerance
- New buildings and extensions at **both North and South Terminals**
- Highways, river works, ancillary facilities

Airfield pavement is constructed inside brutal possession windows because an operating airport cannot stop. Early strength governs when a bay can be trafficked and when the taxiway reopens — which is the cleanest possible Signal argument, and it is worth more here than on almost any building in this sweep.

Gatwick's own workforce forecast names **concrete specialists** among anticipated occupations.

## The route in

No main contractor to approach. But Gatwick refreshed its **Building and Civils Frameworks in June 2026**, appointing 11 firms including Mace, Morgan Sindall and Costain, for up to six years — recorded separately. That framework is the plausible procurement route for elements of this work and is the door available today.

## Gaps

No contractor, no package structure, no pavement specification, no concrete volumes, no programme beyond the 2030 operational target.

## Sources

- Construction Enquirer, 4 August 2026 and 22 September 2025
- London Construction Magazine, August 2026
- Planning Inspectorate, TR020005

On its own content this framework is unpromising: pier refurbishments, EV charging installation, self-check-in enhancements, terminal upgrades. Fit-out and services work, not concrete.

**Will Northern Runway work be let through these frameworks, or procured separately?**

If through: these eleven firms are the buyers for a £2.2bn programme, and this record is the most valuable door in the region.

If separately: it is a list of fit-out contractors.

Nothing published answers it. That is the next action.

The current Southern Construction Framework delivers around **£500m of projects a year** across London, the South East and the South West, and has supported £10bn of public sector construction since 2006.

SCF6 runs an initial four years from **May 2027**, across 10 lots, with value bands reaching **£10m to £100m-plus** for major and complex programmes.

That upper band is where genuine concrete-framed public buildings sit, and it is why this is a Medium rather than the Low most frameworks earn.

SCF6 appointments have not been made — the tender race only just started. The current lists are the best proxy:

**Kier appears on both** — and Kier now has five appearances across this sweep including STEP Fusion and the £1bn Legacy Concrete Roads framework. Morgan Sindall has four.

## Honest caveat

Public sector building — schools, healthcare, civic — uses steel frame and masonry as often as concrete. The £500m a year does not translate into concrete opportunity at anything close to face value.

Nothing until 2027, beyond noting which incumbents Converge already knows.

## Why it qualifies

The largest single concrete opportunity found anywhere in this UK sweep — and the timing is exceptional.

AtkinsRealis states plainly that the objective of the enabling works is to prepare the main construction site for **the deep dig and the first safety-critical concrete pour**. That pour has not happened. On a sixty-year asset with two reactor units, there is no better moment to be in the conversation.

## Concrete scope

- A **cut-off wall of concrete panels extending more than 50m into the ground** around the site perimeter, creating a watertight barrier
- Around **four million cubic metres** of excavation behind it, for the two reactor units
- Nuclear island, conventional island, heat sink, balance of plant, galleries, roads and CRF pipes
- Marine and tunnelling works including **precast concrete heads**

Heidelberg Materials is supplying the main works concrete — 35,000m³ over seven months for the initial cut-off wall phase alone, from an Ipswich plant plus a new on-site mobile batching plant.

## The central obstacle is incumbency, not access

This matters more than anything else in the record.

Sizewell C is explicitly a **near-replica of Hinkley Point C**, deliberately reusing its supply chain, expertise and methods — Heidelberg calls it "intelligent replication". Whatever was specified at Hinkley is the default here.

So the question is not "how do we get in" but "what is already specified, and what would justify changing it". An approach that ignores that will read as naive to anyone on the project.

## The route in

**VolkerWessels is one of Lisa's named accounts and holds two active packages here** — VolkerGround Engineering on the sea defence and haul road, VolkerTrenchless Solutions on HDD landfall and the Combined Drainage Outfall. That is recorded separately and is the strongest available door.

Second route: the **Jaggaer supply chain portal** at sizewellcsupplychain.co.uk publishes current work packages *and a forward view of upcoming procurement*. That forward view is the most valuable public artefact in this file.

## Gaps

No date for the first safety-critical pour. No total concrete volume for the permanent works. No read on whether monitoring is already specified through Hinkley replication — which is the question that determines whether this is winnable.

`Value` deliberately blank: £38bn is a project funding figure, not a construction contract value.

## Sources

- Sizewell C newsroom, 15 January 2026
- New Civil Engineer, 16 January and 2 March 2026
- AtkinsRealis Sizewell C project page
- Heidelberg Materials UK

records.body:
## Why this is the most important record in the file

Not because of its size — the pours here are modest. Because of **who is holding it**.

**VolkerWessels is one of Lisa's named accounts**, and two of its businesses are already appointed and on site at Sizewell C, the largest concrete programme in the country. Under the schema's named-account rule that resolves routing outright, and it converts a cold Tier 1 nuclear approach into a warm one.

## The work itself

**VolkerGround Engineering:**
- 784m temporary sea defence, roughly **12,000 tonnes**
- 343m sheet pile retaining wall, AZ52 and AZ28-700 sections up to 20.2m, for the haul road between the temporary and main construction zones
- Weep holes to relieve pore water pressure

**VolkerTrenchless Solutions:**
- First HDD landfall completed, ~475m of drilling
- CDO auger drill — 54m of 800mm steel casing at a 17-degree entry angle in challenging ground
- **168m³ base plug pour** placed within the CDO shaft
- CDO pipe lining from April 2026, using several vessels and the jack-up barge NP497

Coastal and marine ground engineering in tidal conditions is precisely where early-age behaviour is hardest to predict and most consequential.

## The play

Work VolkerWessels on these packages, **with the wider CWA programme as the prize**. A 168m³ base plug is not the opportunity. Being a known supplier to a named account that is already inside the alliance, before the first safety-critical pour on the nuclear island, is.

## Gaps

No contract values for either VolkerWessels business. No published remaining scope. Unknown whether either has further Sizewell packages in procurement — worth asking directly, since they will know.

## Sources

- New Civil Engineer, 2 March 2026
- VolkerWessels UK, 7 May 2026
- SZC Works Tracker

properties.Name: BOUYGUES TRAVAUX PUBLICS / MURPHY JV - Lower Thames Crossing tunnels and approaches - Thurrock, Essex and Kent
properties.General contractor/JV: Bouygues Travaux Publics — J Murphy & Sons Joint Venture (BMJV). Barbour ABI ranks BMJV the top contractor in the UK in 2026 on the strength of this award. properties.Client: National Highways. Executive director, Lower Thames Crossing: Matt Palmer.

properties.Fit reason: Twin bored road tunnels at 2.6 miles will be the longest in the UK, and at over 16 metres wide among the widest in the world — with a single 16.4m TBM turned around and reused for the second bore. Segmental tunnel lining at that diameter is repeatability at industrial scale, which is the strongest signal in the mass-concrete profile, and the work is genuinely ahead: construction was still only expected to begin during 2026 after the Autumn Budget added £891m. The MixAI case here is stronger than on almost any other record in the sweep, because National Highways has designated LTC a pathfinder project for carbon neutral construction and is explicitly committed to low-carbon concrete and a 70% reduction in construction carbon footprint. That is a mandated, evidenced commitment on a client that has to report against it.
properties.Fit dimensions: Timing: HIGH — contract awarded but main construction still starting during 2026; the tunnel programme is entirely ahead, running six to eight years. Opportunity: HIGH — 2.6 miles of twin bore at 16m+ diameter means a very large segmental lining programme, plus portal buildings and approach structures. Access: MEDIUM — BMJV is identifiable and Murphy is a UK contractor with a public project page, but neither JV member is a Converge account. Coverage: MEDIUM — UK shared patch; note Bouygues is French-parented and also sits in the Sizewell C Civil Works Alliance.
properties.Expected concrete start: Main construction expected to begin during 2026, following DCO consent in March 2025 and an additional £891m of public funding confirmed at the Autumn Budget 2025. Main works are expected to take six to eight years, with opening in the early 2030s.
properties.Summary: The Bouygues Travaux Publics-Murphy Joint Venture holds the Tunnels and Approaches contract on National Highways' Lower Thames Crossing, covering the design and construction of twin road tunnels under the River Thames. At 2.6 miles they will be the longest road tunnels in the UK, and at over 16 metres wide among the widest in the world, carrying three lanes in each direction at national speed limit including double decker HGVs and hydrogen-fuelled vehicles currently restricted at Dartford. A single 16.4m tunnel boring machine will be turned around and reused for the second bore to save cost. The contract also includes tunnel systems, portal buildings and approach roads, plus two ecological habitats, a wetland and two public parks — Tilbury Fields in Thurrock and Chalk Park in Gravesham. The wider £9-11bn scheme connects the A2/M2 in Kent to the A13 and M25 in Thurrock over 23km, 4.2km of it underground. Development consent was granted in March 2025 and an additional £891m of public funding was confirmed at the Autumn Budget 2025. Construction supports up to 22,000 jobs. National Highways has designated it a pathfinder project for carbon neutral construction, committing to low-carbon concrete and steel, hydrogen-powered construction fleets and a 70% reduction in estimated construction carbon footprint.
properties.Notes: AE ROUTING: UNRESOLVED — UK shared patch, neither BMJV member is a named account. CROSS-REGION: the scheme spans Thurrock/Essex and Kent. This record and the Balfour Beatty Roads North record are filed under East of England. SKANSKA'S £450m KENT ROADS PACKAGE IS DELIBERATELY NOT RECORDED HERE — create it when the South East is swept, and note Skanska is an Aled named account, so that record will route cleanly. NEXT ACTION (25 Aug 2026): the MixAI angle is unusually strong and should lead. National Highways is publicly committed to carbon neutral construction with low-carbon concrete and a 70% footprint reduction, and has run supply chain roadshows (sixty local firms attended the first at South Essex College in Grays, January 2026). VALUE CONFLICT: the tunnels contract is variously reported at £1.3bn, £1.34bn and £2.3bn (the last described as estimated value at award of preferred contractor status). £1300 entered as the most commonly cited figure; treat the band rather than the number. CONFIRMED (Murphy Group project page; National Highways; Construction Enquirer 25 Mar 2025; Traffic Technology Today; Born To Engineer; NCE 2 Jul 2026): BMJV composition and scope, 2.6-mile twin bores as longest UK road tunnels, 16m+ width, 16.4m TBM turned and reused, tunnel systems and portal buildings and approach roads, ecological habitats and Tilbury Fields and Chalk Park, 23km route with 4.2km underground, DCO March 2025, £891m Autumn Budget 2025 addition, 2026 construction start, six to eight year main works, early 2030s opening, 22,000 jobs, carbon neutral pathfinder designation with low-carbon concrete and steel and hydrogen plant and 70% footprint reduction target, £60m insurance procurement running 30 Nov 2026 to 19 Nov 2033, Barbour ABI top UK contractor ranking. INFERRED: that segmental precast lining is the dominant concrete element — true of bored road tunnels, not itemised for LTC. NOT CONFIRMED: segment supplier or casting location, segment count, concrete volumes, whether main construction has actually started.

records.body:
## Why it qualifies

Twin bored road tunnels, **2.6 miles — the longest in the UK** — and at over 16 metres wide, among the widest in the world. A single **16.4m TBM** will be turned around and reused for the second bore.

Segmental lining at that diameter is repeatability at industrial scale, which is the strongest signal in the mass-concrete profile. And the programme is genuinely ahead: main construction was still only expected to begin during 2026 after the Autumn Budget added £891m, with six to eight years of main works to follow.

## Lead with carbon here

This is the strongest MixAI case in the entire sweep, and it is not close.

National Highways has designated LTC a **pathfinder project for carbon neutral construction**, committing publicly to **low-carbon concrete and steel**, hydrogen-powered construction fleets, and a **70% reduction in estimated construction carbon footprint**. They have separately procured low-carbon hydrogen supply as a distinct contract.

That is a mandated, evidenced commitment on a public client who has to report against it — not a BREEAM rating or an operational-energy claim like most of the residential records in this sweep.

## Concrete scope

- Segmental precast lining for 2.6 miles of twin 16m+ bore
- Portal buildings and approach structures
- Tunnel systems

No segment supplier or casting location is published. That is the first thing to establish — compare with STRABAG's Hartlepool plant for HS2 and Explore's Worksop plant, both recorded elsewhere in this sweep.

## Value health warning

Reported at £1.3bn, £1.34bn and £2.3bn across sources (the last described as estimated value at award of preferred contractor status). £1,300 entered as the most commonly cited. **Use the band, not the number.**

## Cross-region

Spans Thurrock/Essex and Kent. This record and Balfour Beatty's Roads North are filed here. **Skanska's £450m Kent Roads package is deliberately not recorded** — create it in the South East sweep, where it will route cleanly to Aled as a named account.

## Sources

- Murphy Group project page
- National Highways LTC pages
- Construction Enquirer, 25 March 2025
- New Civil Engineer, 2 July 2026

records.body:
## Why a producer record scores High

Heidelberg holds the **main works concrete supply** for Sizewell C — the largest concrete programme in the country — and is running a **dedicated on-site mobile batching plant** alongside supply from Ipswich.

Captive on-site batching on a nuclear project is close to the ideal MixAI environment:

- The producer controls the mix
- The plant is dedicated to one client for a decade-plus
- Volumes are enormous and continuing
- Nuclear QA makes the evidence trail contractual, not optional

## They are already optimising

The mix contains **Sika admixtures** engineered for three specific things: workability, a longer window for placing and compaction, and inhibiting groundwater ingress.

That matters for how to open the conversation. Someone here is already engineering mix behaviour deliberately — so this is not a pitch about why mix optimisation matters. It is a conversation about better data on something they are already doing, with a technical counterpart who will understand it immediately.

It also means Sika has an established technical relationship that has to be worked with rather than around.

## Current scope

~35,000m³ over seven months for the **initial phase of the cut-off wall** — concrete panels extending more than 50m into the ground, forming the watertight barrier that enables four million cubic metres of excavation.

That is the initial phase of one structure. The permanent works are entirely ahead.

## Routing note

Heidelberg Materials is German-parented. Given the Hinkley-to-Sizewell "intelligent replication" model, a **group-level conversation may be more productive than a site one** — and that would touch Lisa's Continental Europe patch. Flagged, not decided.

## Two suppliers, two conversations

Heidelberg on main works; **Eastern Concrete** on enabling and early works (120,000m³, recorded separately). Very different scales, both worth having.

## Sources

- Heidelberg Materials UK, October 2025

records.body:
## Why this might be the first call on the whole Sizewell programme

Not the biggest contract. The **most reachable counterpart**.

Eastern Concrete is a Suffolk independent supplying **over 120,000m³ over two years** from a dedicated Leiston plant, with a second plant planned on the construction site. Managing director **Tom Baker** described it publicly as "the biggest contract I've ever secured and the highlight of my career".

That is a completely different conversation from a Tier 1 procurement function or a multinational producer's nuclear team. Small enough to decide quickly. Invested enough to care about delivering well. Actively expanding capacity for this specific work.

## Why the batching environment is good

**Two dedicated plants serving one client for two years.** That is about as controlled and repeatable as ready-mix supply gets — consistent mixes, consistent aggregates, a single delivery destination, and a producer with every incentive to get consistency right because their reputation is riding on the largest job they have ever done.

## The scope distinction matters

Eastern Concrete's material supports **non-nuclear** activities: site roads, park and ride facilities, temporary buildings. Heidelberg holds the main works and the cut-off wall.

That cuts both ways. Lighter QA requirements mean less contractual pull for evidence — but also **far fewer regulatory barriers to trying something new**. On a nuclear licensed structure, changing anything is a formal process. On a park and ride slab, it isn't.

## Two producers, one project

- **Heidelberg Materials** — main works, cut-off wall, on-site mobile plant (recorded separately)
- **Eastern Concrete** — enabling and early works, 120,000m³, Leiston plant

Different scales, different barriers. Start here.

## Sources

- Sizewell C newsroom, September 2025
- Construction Enquirer, 8 July 2025

## Why a £30m job earns a Medium

Because the substructure is disproportionately concrete-heavy for the value:

- **Over 5,000 precast piles**, each around 28m long
- A **1.2m deep reinforced concrete raft** on top of them

A 1.2m raft is thick enough for early-age thermal behaviour to matter. 5,000 piles at 28m is a repeatable driven-pile programme. The concrete is concentrated in the ground — which is also where it is least forgiving and least visible.

## What's above ground isn't for us

A 12-storey automated container stacking facility rising to 55m across 323m by 159m: 15,000 tonnes of steelwork, 50,000 sq m of cladding, a 46,500 sq m roof. That is a steel job.

So the pitch is narrow and specific: the raft and the piling, not the building.

## Timing

Bids invited, no contractor appointed. Method unfixed, winner knowable soon. The substructure is let inside the main contract, so **whoever wins is the buyer**.

This was surfaced during the London sweep and flagged as out-of-region. London Gateway is in Thurrock, Essex — it belongs here. Don't duplicate it in the London file.

Dry dock and berth reconstruction is about as pure a mass-concrete opportunity as exists: **extremely thick sections, marine and tidal exposure, nuclear-licensed consequence of failure**, and structures that must stay watertight for decades.

The £750m SDA contract sits inside a **ten-year site-wide programme** at the largest naval support site in Western Europe.

- **Kier BAM** — main works contractor on 10 Dock

- **Mace** — advisory on 5 Basin Berth
- **Babcock** — owner, operator, licensee

Three of those four recur elsewhere in this sweep.

## The obstacle: vetting

This is a Defence Nuclear Enterprise site. Security vetting is a genuine barrier that will add months to any engagement, and job adverts for the site require Devonport Dockyard Baseline Personal Security before anyone sets foot on it.

Factor that into any pipeline forecast. A deal here is slow even when it works.

- **Kier** — six appearances (STEP Fusion, Legacy Concrete Roads framework, YORbuild 2, Sizewell North Plaza, SCF incumbent, Kier BAM here)

properties.General contractor/JV: BYLOR, the joint venture of Bouygues Travaux Publics and Laing O'Rourke, as main civils contractor. BYLOR operates the on-site concrete production plants. MEH Alliance (Altrad, Balfour Beatty Bailey, Cavendish Nuclear, Doosan Babcock) delivers mechanical, electrical and HVAC. Kier BAM also worked on the project. Kilnbridge delivered the underwater concrete heads at Avonmouth.
properties.Concrete subcontractor: BYLOR self-delivers and operates the on-site batching plants. Raw materials supplied by Hanson (Heidelberg Materials UK); mix design developed jointly by Sika, BYLOR and Hanson.
properties.Client: NNB Generation Company (HPC) Limited, financed by EDF Energy and China General Nuclear Power Group. Project delivery director: Simon Parsons. Nuclear island area director: Simon Parsons. Regulator: Office for Nuclear Regulation.
properties.Location: Hinkley Point, Somerset, on the Severn Estuary — plus the Avonmouth casting yard for marine concrete heads
properties.Competitor present: Assume heavily instrumented. Sika has a seven-year mix development relationship, BYLOR runs the batching plants with moisture control to plus or minus 0.2%, and every batch must comply with stringent EDF and ONR requirements. This is the most technically mature concrete operation in the UK and it did not get that way without measurement.
properties.Fit reason: An honest read on timing rather than scale. The headline numbers are extraordinary — around one million cubic metres of nuclear-quality concrete over the build, 850,000m3 already poured by 2021, and two successive UK continuous-pour records at 9,000m3 and 8,991m3 for the Unit 1 and Unit 2 basemats in 2019 and 2020. But those are historic. Unit 1 has shifted from heavy component installation to internal fit-out, Unit 2 is completing its buildings after a dome lift, and prefabricated elements now make up around 60% of the build. The concrete phase is largely behind us, and grading this High on volume would be exactly the size-is-not-fit error. It is a Medium, and its real value is strategic: HPC is the reference case that Sizewell C is deliberately replicating, so the specification and monitoring decisions made here govern what happens in Suffolk.
properties.Fit dimensions: Timing: LOW-MEDIUM — basemats complete since 2020, Unit 1 in fit-out, Unit 2 completing buildings, prefabrication at ~60%. The pours are largely done. Opportunity: MEDIUM — residual structural work continues on Unit 2 and across the balance of plant, but the repeatable headline pours have passed. Access: MEDIUM-HIGH — BYLOR, Hanson and Sika are all identifiable with named technical leadership. Coverage: MEDIUM — UK shared patch; both BYLOR parents are large international groups.
properties.Expected concrete start: Largely complete. Unit 1 basemat J-zero achieved June 2019, Unit 2 June 2020. Unit 1 is now in internal fit-out; Unit 2 is completing buildings following a dome lift. Commissioning targeted 2030 on the Wikipedia entry, against earlier public statements of 2026-2027.
properties.Summary: Hinkley Point C is a two-unit, 3,200MWe EPR nuclear power station under construction in Somerset since March 2017, financed by EDF Energy and China General Nuclear Power Group, with construction cost given as £35bn in 2015 prices (around £48bn in 2026 prices) and 6,300 on-site construction workers. BYLOR, the Bouygues Travaux Publics and Laing O'Rourke joint venture, is main civils contractor and operates the on-site concrete production plants. Around one million cubic metres of nuclear-quality concrete is required over the build; 850,000m3 had been poured by 2021 alongside 5.3 million cubic metres of earth moved. The Unit 1 nuclear island basemat was completed in June 2019 with a 9,000m3 five-day continuous pour setting an English record, and the Unit 2 49,000-tonne basemat was completed in June 2020 with an 8,991m3 pour setting a UK record. Sika, BYLOR and Hanson jointly developed the concrete mixes over more than seven years to meet EDF and ONR requirements, with batching plants controlling sand and aggregate moisture to plus or minus 0.2%. Kilnbridge cast six 5,000-tonne underwater reinforced concrete heads at Avonmouth for the marine works. records.body:
## Why it qualifies

The rare record where **the remaining pour is quantified in public**.

HS2 states sub-surface work needs **69,000m³ of concrete and 19,000t of reinforcement** in total. As at March 2026, **29,000m³ and 7,000t had been placed**. That leaves roughly **40,000m³ still to pour on sub-surface alone** — arithmetic, not a published figure, but the arithmetic is shown.

And that is before the deck. Platform construction began June 2026: **188 concrete piers** carrying a **144,000 sq ft deck** across a 450m station.

## Concrete scope

- ~40,000m³ of sub-surface concrete remaining
- 188 piers and the deck structure
- 500+ precast beams, 7-34m long, 14-58t, from Shay Murtagh Precast in Ireland — a separate precast angle
- Piling complete (2,000+ piles to 24m), so everything structural above it is ahead

## Entry angle — go at MPB, not MDJV

**MPB Structures** holds the substructure package: 417 pile caps, ~17,000m³ of concrete, 4,700t of rebar, 140 people on site. They are **Birmingham-based with a named business owner (Patrick Boyle)** who talks publicly about local employment and social value.

That is a far shorter route to a decision than a Mace/Dragados JV procurement function. And MPB also holds the **Bromford Tunnel West Portal** — one relationship covers two HS2 structures in the same region.

## Secondary angle

BREEAM Excellent and net zero carbon in operation, with Mace publicly describing an "ambitious low carbon strategy". Worth testing whether that extends to embodied carbon — unlike most records in this sweep, a BREEAM Excellent target on a public infrastructure project usually does.

## Health warnings

**Dates conflict.** Railway News (May 2026) says opening 2029-2033. Place Midlands (June 2026) says the railway will not open before 2036. Treating 2036 as current.

**HS2 is 18 months into a reset**, with a new cost and schedule to be agreed with government during 2026. Every date here is provisional.

Assume incumbent instrumentation. HS2 runs monitoring across the programme and it would be careless to pitch into it blind.

## Sources

- Place Midlands, 24 June 2026 (platform deck)
- Railway Supply, 5 March 2026 (piling complete, volumes)
- New Civil Engineer, 5 February 2025 (MPB scope)
- Ground Engineering, 7 February 2025

Cross passages. The same small structure many times over, in a confined environment where early strength governs when the next access can happen. That is a better Signal case than the tunnel lining itself at this stage.

The 750m cut-and-cover West Portal — the deepest of four Midlands portals — took **5,000t of reinforcement and 28,000m³ of concrete** from MPB Structures since March 2023.

## Why it qualifies

Birmingham's largest city centre redevelopment and, on Place Midlands' framing, one of Europe's largest regeneration schemes. **Near £2bn, 3,000 homes, 42 acres, four phases over a decade.** Outline unanimously approved June 2025, construction due to start during 2026, archaeology already done in late 2025.

## Why the decade matters more than the value

A relationship established at phase one carries through nine more years of pours with the same development partner. That is worth considerably more than any individual building, and it is the reason this scores High despite having no contractor named.

Compare it to a £300m tower: bigger number here, but the real prize is being the incumbent when phases two, three and four are specified.

## The question that decides everything

**Is Lendlease self-delivering phase one, or appointing a main contractor?**

Lendlease has its own construction arm. If they self-deliver, the buyer is Lendlease and the conversation is with one organisation for ten years. If they appoint, the buyer changes phase by phase and the value of an early relationship drops sharply.

Nothing published answers this. It is the first thing to establish.

## Routing note

Lendlease is Australian-parented. If a group relationship develops rather than a Birmingham site one, it may touch Jeremy's APAC patch. Flagged, not decided.

## Gaps

No contractor, no phase boundaries, no storey heights, no structural systems, no unit mix, no confirmation that structural work has actually started.

## Not the usual worthless framework

Frameworks normally cap out at Low here. This one earns a Medium for a specific reason: **work may be delivered on an early contractor involvement basis**, and that is written into the framework terms rather than being something to hope for.

ECI is the entry point the scoring model rewards, and here it is advertised.

## The scale

£980m excluding VAT (£1.17bn including) over eight years from April 2026, with Birmingham City Council alone accounting for £640m. Highways and infrastructure means **bridges, culverts, retaining structures and carriageway reconstruction** — real structural concrete, not the sub-£500k small works that made the Wirral framework in the North West file worthless.

## The shortest target list in the region

The lot structure is the useful part:

- Lot one: max 10 firms
- Lot two: max 6
- Lots three and five: max 3 each
- **Lot four: max 2**

Two firms on the highest-value band. If those two names can be resolved, that is the shortest possible target list for large Midlands civils work for the next eight years.

**The appointee list was not resolved in this sweep, and it is the only genuinely useful output.** That is the next action.

## Worth knowing alongside

The companion £200m Transportation and Infrastructure Professional Services Framework went to **AtkinsRealis, Jacobs, Mott MacDonald and Pell Frischmann**, running to 2034. Designers specify structures — four names covering Midlands highways design for eight years is worth having.

## Cross-region

## Why it qualifies

A **625ft tower** plus an 8-storey shoulder building, 506 student beds, targeting a **September 2028 opening**.

An academic-year deadline is the hardest external deadline the scoring model recognises — students arrive on a fixed date. And working backwards from September 2028, the frame has to be under way well before then, which means **the contractor appointment is imminent**.

## The market context is unusually solid

Birmingham city centre faces a predicted shortfall of around **5,000 student beds**. That makes the demand behind this structural rather than speculative — which matters in a year when residential tower delivery elsewhere is fragile.

The neighbouring 29-storey **Vita Tower** (540 beds) is already under construction, so there is a live PBSA cluster here rather than an isolated scheme.

## The faster route

Identify the **Vita Tower contractor**. They are on the ground next door, building the same product to the same market, and they are a plausible bidder here. That is a shorter path than waiting for the Landmark appointment.

## Gaps

No contractor. No confirmation approval was actually granted — the source has it at "set for green light". No structural system, value, programme, or even a storey count for the main tower (the height is given in feet only).

## Sources

- Place Midlands, 18 March 2026

records.body:
## Why it qualifies

A **62,000-capacity stadium with a retractable pitch**, plus a 15,000-20,000 capacity arena and a show pitch, across 48 acres. If it proceeds, one of the largest single concrete opportunities in the region.

## The typology is genuinely good

Stadium construction is dominated by **precast terracing units and raker beams** — the same unit repeated hundreds of times. That is the strongest signal in the mass-concrete profile, and a stand is essentially one pour design multiplied.

A **retractable pitch** adds something unusual: substantial substructure to house the mechanism, which is deep, heavy and one-off rather than repetitive.

## What's solid and what isn't

Solid: Knighthead **completed the purchase in 2024**. The land is owned, not optioned, which puts this ahead of most speculative mega-schemes.

Not solid: no contractor, no designer, no value, no programme, no established planning position. Everything above about concrete is typology, not fact.

## Three stadium records now

Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium (Laing O'Rourke, with Banagher Precast Concrete and Expanded Structures) in the North West file, Elland Road in the Yorkshire file, and this. **A sector view may be worth more than three separate pursuits** — the precast supply chain for UK stadiums is small, and Banagher is already a named name in it.

## What to do

One search: planning status and whether any contractor or design team is appointed. If a Tier 1 is on board this becomes a High immediately.

## Sources

- Place Midlands, September 2025

records.body:
## Why it qualifies

Best-timed opportunity in the East Midlands and one of the best in the whole UK sweep — but not for the usual reason. There is nothing to pour yet.

ILIOS was appointed Construction Partner in **March 2026**, five months ago, and its published remit explicitly includes **supply chain management and development, both regionally around West Burton and nationally**. That is a stated intention to build a concrete supply chain, with a named programme director attached, happening right now.

## The scale behind the £200m

£200m is only the **first three-year tranche**. Kier's own statement describes the wider programme as carrying future opportunities of **up to £10bn**, against a record £2.5bn of government fusion investment over five years including £1.3bn to STEP. Peak construction supports 8,000 onsite jobs.

## Why the concrete matters

A tokamak building is the mass-concrete profile at its most extreme: **very thick shielded sections, exceptionally high consequence of failure**, and a nuclear-adjacent QA regime where evidence is contractual rather than discretionary. Nuvia's presence in the consortium is the tell — they are a nuclear specialist, and they are there because this is nuclear-grade civils.

## Honest position on timing

The DCO application is still in preparation. Non-statutory consultation ran January to March 2026, and long-term Trent water level risk is still being assessed as an input to design and site layout. **First pours are years away.**

That is not a weakness here — it is the point. This is the pre-method window the scoring model says is the best moment, caught unusually early, on a programme with a forty-year horizon.

## Kier is becoming an account

Three live long-term Kier programmes across this sweep:

- STEP Fusion construction partner (this record)
- National Highways **£1bn Legacy Concrete Roads Reconstruction** framework, 2026-2032, with Graham and Sisk
- YORbuild Major Works 2

Worth raising at triage as an account rather than three pursuits.

## Gaps

No concrete volumes. No DCO submission date. No first pour date. And it is unclear whether the £200m tranche includes any physical construction at all or is entirely design and site readiness — worth establishing early.

## Sources

- Nuclear Industry Association, 23 March 2026
- Sharecast / Kier statement, 16 March 2026
- Turner & Townsend consortium announcement
- STEP Fusion FAQs and West Burton pages

## Why it qualifies

The largest East Midlands industrial scheme to come forward in 2025. **4.5m sq ft total, phase one around 2m sq ft**, due to start early 2026 with hybrid planning granted in December 2025 — and with an occupier lined up in advance.

A pre-let means a hard handover date, which is the deadline pressure the model rewards.

~2m sq ft of power-floated ground-bearing slab in a single building is a genuinely large pour programme. Early trafficking and joint layout drive the sequence, and slab flatness tolerances on a modern distribution centre are tight because of high-bay racking.

Logistics slabs are a **commoditised, price-led** part of the market. High volume, low value per cubic metre, and the party pouring usually competes on rate rather than programme certainty. The same caveat applies to Follingsby Park in the North East file.

Medium is where this honestly lands: real volume, real deadline, difficult economics.

- **YORbuild Major Works 2 lot one** — public sector call-offs across three regions

One group, two regions, three routes in. Worth an account conversation rather than three project pursuits.

Is Caddick Construction delivering Em.Ex, or is a third-party contractor appointed? The group structure makes self-delivery possible and that single answer determines who the buyer is.

## A producer, not a project

The only clear example of the **precast and batching supply** profile found in the East Midlands.

Explore Manufacturing's Worksop plant made **1,946 precast platform slabs** — up to 4m by 2m, 4-5 tonnes each — for HS2's Old Oak Common station.

## Why factory precast is the ideal environment

In a controlled plant, **curing cycle directly governs throughput**. Demould too early and you crack units; demould too late and you lose a bed turn. That is the cleanest possible Signal argument — no weather, no site variability, and a production manager who already measures cycle time daily because it is their whole job.

## Why Medium

The Old Oak Common run is finished, and no current or forward order book is published. Without knowing what the plant is making now, the timing dimension can't be scored.

## Two UK precast plants supplying HS2

Worth reading together:

- **Explore, Worksop** — 1,946 platform slabs for Old Oak Common (this record)
- **STRABAG, Hartlepool** — 48,294 tunnel segments for the Euston Tunnel (London file)

Both are producer-side conversations with the same shape, and STRABAG is already a named Lisa account.

## Verify before working

Explore sitting within Laing O'Rourke is general knowledge rather than something sourced in this sweep. Check it.

records.body:
## Why it qualifies

The procurement structure is the reason this is a High.

The successful contractor is **initially appointed to help Network Rail refine construction methodologies and establish target costs** before main construction is authorised. That is an explicit ECI phase — the exact moment the scoring model calls the best entry point — and unusually it is being advertised in advance rather than having to be caught by luck.

## Concrete scope

- Tunnel track lowering and **slab track installation through three tunnels**
- W12 gauge clearance
- A new third line between Standedge and Gledholt
- Electrification enabling works

Slab track is repetitive and tolerance-critical, and early strength governs when track can be loaded and the possession handed back. On a railway, **possession windows are the hardest external deadline that exists** — harder than a rent clock or an academic year, because overrunning one has regulatory and compensation consequences the same day.

## The problem, and the play

There is no contractor to talk to. Award is not until March 2027.

So the play is not to sell — it is to **identify the four shortlisted bidders in Q4 2026** and be known to them while they are building their methodology and target cost. A supplier that helps a bidder's ECI case is in a different position from one who calls after the award.

Several likely bidders (Morgan Sindall, BAM Nuttall, Balfour Beatty) would also resolve the AE routing question the moment one wins.

## Honest caveats

Main construction is **subject to funding approval** in the notice's own words. This is not a certainty, and the eight-year term to 2035 means anything could happen to the back end.

Cross-region: the package runs Stalybridge (Greater Manchester) to Huddersfield (West Yorkshire). Filed here — don't duplicate it in the North West.

- Find a Tender, notice 2026/S 000-053834

Caddick Group holds **both the development and the contracting businesses**. Caddick Developments is the developer here; Caddick Construction is a contractor in its own right and sits on YORbuild Major Works 2.

**Approach Caddick Group, not this scheme.** Two doors into the same organisation: their own development pipeline, and their YORbuild Major Works 2 lot one place giving them public-sector call-offs across Yorkshire, the North East and the East Midlands.

## Why it qualifies

45 storeys — the **tallest building in Yorkshire** if built — with 464 build-to-rent homes and around 364,000 sq ft of workspace on a 2.47-acre West End site. McLaren is a developer-contractor group, so the self-delivery advantage may apply.

## The problem: the source is two years old

This record rests on an **April 2024** article which said initial work was set to start later that year. Nothing found in this sweep confirms a start.

That matters more than usual right now. London Construction Magazine's 2026 analysis is blunt that consented residential towers are seeing tender disengagement rather than tender competition, and a consented scheme is not a deliverable scheme. A 45-storey BTR tower approved in 2024 with no confirmed start is exactly the profile that stalls.

**Verify status before any approach.**

## Context worth having anyway

Leeds has a real tower cluster forming: 33 storeys at the former International Pool, 42 storeys of student at the former Yorkshire Post site, 31 at Skinner Street, and the 45-storey Cirrus Point student scheme at Merrion Way.

McLaren also has Beck Yard in the city — £85m, 375 homes, started earlier. If Wellington Square is stalled, Beck Yard may not be, and McLaren is still worth a conversation as a group.

## Overlap check

Wellington Square sits on Wellington Street **and Lisbon Street**. The Winvic £130m BTR record is on Lisbon Street. Resolve whether these are neighbouring or overlapping parcels before working both.

## Sources

- Insider Media Yorkshire, 12 April 2024
- Building, 15 April 2024

## Why it qualifies

A live concrete programme on the ground, not a framework: a replacement station, a new **Calder Road bridge** built with 20 precast concrete beams, and the **Baker Viaduct**, all progressing through 2026.

Rail structures run to possession windows, which is the hardest deadline type in construction — overrunning one has compensation consequences the same day.

## Why Medium

The Calder Road beams are already installed and parapets are being fitted, so a meaningful share of that structure's pours has passed. The Baker Viaduct and the station still have work ahead, but this is a mid-programme record rather than a pre-start one.

## The gap that matters most

**No project-specific contractor.** The names in this record — Morgan Sindall Infrastructure, BAM Nuttall, Balfour Beatty Rail, Spencer Group — come from a programme-level article about OLE and portfolio work, not from Ravensthorpe. They are recorded as context, not as the project team.

Resolving the TRU West civils contractor is the single most useful next step in this file, because it probably unlocks several Yorkshire TRU structures at once rather than just this one.

## Programme context

TRU spans 12 stations, 70 miles of track, 65 bridges and 6 tunnels, with around 120 route km of new 25kV OLE. The civil works enabling electrification — bridge headroom modifications, tunnel relining, embankment widening — are substantial in aggregate even where individual structures are modest.

## Sources

- New Civil Engineer, 29 January 2026

records.body:
## Why it is here at all

£1.04bn, 1,400MW, 3,100MWh — the largest battery storage hub in the UK and one of the largest in Europe.

Battery storage looks like a non-opportunity for concrete, and dismissing it would be the easy call.

## The reason not to dismiss it

**Repeatability.** A site at this capacity means hundreds of near-identical container plinths and foundation pads, laid to consistent tolerance across a large area. The scoring model is explicit that repeatability is the strongest signal in the mass-concrete profile — a scheme with 100 near-identical pours is worth far more than a one-off pour of the same volume, because a saving multiplies.

That argument holds even though each individual pour is small.

## The honest counterweight

The £1.04bn is dominated by battery hardware and grid connection, not civils. Total concrete volume is modest against that headline, and treating the project value as the opportunity size would be exactly the error the model warns about.

Construction also **began in 2025**, so foundations may already be well advanced or finished.

## The blocker

No construction contractor identified. This record is built from an encyclopaedia entry — the technical figures are reliable, the construction detail is simply absent. One search should fix it, and nothing can be done here until it does.

## Sources

- Wikipedia, Thorpe Marsh Green Energy Hub (sourced entry)
- Barbour ABI Yorkshire & the Humber league table (£435m figure for a Thorpe Marsh Power Station project, which does not reconcile with the £1.04bn above — treat both cautiously)

## Not a project — but not the usual worthless framework either

Frameworks normally score Low here. This one earns a Medium for two reasons.

**Lot 2 is £900m of schemes above £30m.** That is a substantial band, unlike the Wirral framework in the North West file where the tender volumes showed everything concentrated below £1m.

**It runs to 2032 across three English regions** — Yorkshire and the Humber, the North East, and Lincolnshire, Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire and parts of Leicestershire — with eight contractors per lot. It is effectively a map of who will build public sector work across half of northern England for the next six years.

## The lot 1 list

Caddick Construction, Galliford Try, Kier, Morgan Sindall Construction & Infrastructure, Robertson Construction Group, Tilbury Douglas, Vinci Building, Wates.

Several of these recur across this sweep. **Caddick appears here and on South Village** — one relationship covers their own £1bn development pipeline and their public-sector call-offs.

## The gap worth closing

**The lot 2 list is not published in the sources reviewed** — and lot 2 is the £900m band with the larger schemes. That is the more valuable of the two lists and the obvious next question.

## Honest caveat

Public sector building — education, healthcare, civic — skews to steel frame and masonry as often as to concrete. The framework value does not translate into concrete opportunity at anything like face value.

## Cross-region

Covers the North East and East Midlands too. Filed here; don't duplicate it when those regions are swept.

## Sources

- Construction News, 24 June 2026
- New Civil Engineer, 29 June and 17 July 2026

records.body:
## Why it qualifies

The largest vertical concrete programme found anywhere in the UK outside London. Five towers, **2,400 homes**, a 71-storey Lighthouse tower that would be the tallest building in the country outside the capital, and a published build cost of **£894.5m** against £1.1bn GDV.

Every dimension points the same way, which is rare enough to be worth stating plainly.

## The delivery model is the argument

Renaker self-delivers. There is no main contractor arguing with a frame subcontractor about who benefits from a faster cycle — the developer, the builder and the party carrying the programme risk are one organisation. That is the cleanest possible buying structure for Cure/Signal.

They also run **MEVA MAC hydraulic automatic climbing** on core walls for everything above 30 storeys, chosen specifically to make core construction crane-independent. A contractor that has already engineered its core cycle to that degree is not being sold the idea that cycle time matters; they are being sold better data about it.

## Concrete scope

- Lighthouse: 71 storeys, 642 apartments
- The Green: two 47-storey towers and two at 51 storeys
- 2,400 homes across the cluster, repeating residential floorplate throughout

## Entry angle

Work **Renaker as an account, not this cluster as a project**. They have 1,534 homes and 861 student beds already under construction completing 2027-2029, three schemes started since October 2025, and three more flagged for 2026 starts. A result on core and slab cycle is portable across all of it.

Aled owns the account.

## Gaps

No tower-by-tower start dates. No concrete volumes or current cycle figures. The S106 viability position — Renaker argued it could not afford any affordable housing contribution — signals real cost pressure, which makes a cycle-time saving easier to sell and a low-carbon premium harder.

- Place North West, September 2024 (tower composition)
- Construction Enquirer, 13 April 2026 (results, pipeline)
- MEVA UK project pages (MAC climbing system on Renaker cores)

The only clear DfMA record in the North West sweep. An **£85m government construction pilot** in Liverpool City Region, with Starship — a developer, contractor and MMC specialist — named as a participant.

No project list, no sites, no unit numbers, no programme. Pilots routinely deliver less than they announce.

That single question determines whether the record is worth anything, and it should be answered before anything else is done with it.

To Avi, on product grounds rather than geography — the schema tiebreaker is explicit that DfMA at PCSA stage points to Avi.

records.body:
## Why it qualifies

The best access position found anywhere in this sweep so far. **Unite Students is one of Aled's named accounts** — and here they are not a tenant or a distant client but the majority JV partner, developer, asset manager and operator with 51%. Coverage is resolved outright and the relationship route already exists.

The timing is real too. Gateway 2 approved, JV and funding closed in December 2025, the first building's cores completed April 2026, and **eight floors still to pour on building one with a second building entirely ahead**, running to 2029/30.

## The deadline does the selling

788 beds must be occupiable for the start of the **2028/29 academic year**. 1,221 more for **2029/30**.

Students arrive on a fixed date whether the building is finished or not. There is no softer deadline type in UK construction, and Unite's whole business model depends on hitting it.

## Read this before the first call — the frame is steel

Newcastle University's own March 2026 update is explicit: cores installed first, then **the structural steel frame**, then the first of eight floors poured.

So the concrete packages here are cores, substructure and composite floor slabs — not a concrete frame. Walking in with a concrete-frame cycle pitch would be wrong and would be spotted immediately. The right pitch is floor pour cycle on a repeating plate above a steel frame, plus the cores.

Good news for repeatability regardless: two buildings, each sub-divided into 12 blocks, four to nine storeys. The same floor happens many times.

## Entry angle

Through Unite Students, not Bowmer + Kirkland cold. Unite has a national development pipeline and B+K has already delivered 3,000 rooms for them across the UK — a result here is portable to both organisations at once.

## Don't lead with carbon

The target is **Net Zero Carbon in Operation** — gas-free, electrification, on-site generation, ASHPs. All operational. No published embodied-carbon commitment, so MixAI has no hook.

## Gaps

No concrete volumes, no floor cycle target, no frame subcontractor named.

## Sources

- Construction News, 29 January 2026
- Newcastle University press office, December 2025 and March 2026
- Place North East, 6 January 2026
- Bowmer + Kirkland newsroom; NORR project page

## Why it qualifies

A **742MW CCGT with 2Mtpa carbon capture** is heavy industrial civils: turbine hall foundations, absorber and compressor bases, tank foundations and pipe racks. Thick sections, high consequence of failure, and demanding tolerance on machine bases where a foundation problem stops a turbine.

Construction started mid-2025 for 2028 operations, so a large share of the programme is live right now.

## Access is unusually good for something this size

**Balfour Beatty** is named construction partner. **Costain** holds a separate EPC for the CO2 gathering system and gas connection, having done the FEED.

And Costain now appears **three times across this whole UK sweep** — Sellafield IDP utilities partner, the TfL £700m station framework in London, and here. Three live long-term programmes with one contractor is an account argument, not three project pursuits. Worth raising at triage.

## MixAI has a real hook here

Unlike most records in this sweep where carbon is a rating target, **the entire commercial rationale of this project is carbon reduction**. It is a Track-1 CCUS project backed by government money on the basis of tonnes captured. Embodied carbon in the civils is a live question for people who have to answer to DESNZ, not a nice-to-have.

## Honest caveats

Construction began mid-2025, so foundations are partly done. Nobody has published how much of the civils programme remains, and the answer materially changes the timing score.

No concrete volumes anywhere. No civils subcontractor named. Assume structural monitoring is already specified on a project with this regulatory profile and check rather than pitching blind.

## Why it qualifies

**Up to ten data centre buildings totalling 540,000 sq m on one campus.** That is the largest repeatable slab and raft programme found anywhere in this UK sweep.

Repeatability is the strongest signal in the mass-concrete profile — the scoring model is explicit that a hundred near-identical pours beat a one-off pour of the same volume, because a saving multiplies. Ten near-identical buildings is that argument at building scale, before counting substations, generator bases and ancillary structures.

## The timing is the reason it's a High and not a watch record

Phase A enabling works — compounds, clearance, fencing, extensive earthworks — run in stages **over 16 months to autumn 2026**. That means the main works procurement is happening approximately now, and **no vertical contractor is appointed yet**.

Being known before that appointment is worth more than anything that can be done after it.

## What Phase A tells us

The first reserved matters approval covers 54 hectares of enabling work only. Nothing structural has been consented in detail yet. That is a genuine constraint on how quickly this becomes real, and worth saying out loud rather than treating £10bn as if it were purchasable today.

## Access is the weak dimension

There is nobody to sell to. Blackstone-owned hyperscale developers procure through their own channels, and QTS is US-parented — **if a relationship develops group-side rather than site-side, this may not be a UK territory account at all**. Flagged, not decided.

## Gaps

No main contractor. No per-building floor areas. No concrete volumes, slab specification or tolerance requirements. No confirmation that all ten buildings proceed.

## Sources

- Construction Enquirer, 26 August 2025
- Place North East, December 2025 watchlist
- Glenigan, North East activity

## A site, not a project

4,500 acres across Redcar and Teesside, £500m+ public investment, several billion in private commitment. That cannot be scored as a project, and treating the headline as an opportunity size would be meaningless.

## Why it earns a Medium anyway

It is the **physical platform underneath several other records in this file**. Net Zero Teesside is here. The East Coast Cluster supply chain is concentrated here — Cavendish Northern at Billingham, px group, Adey Steel. Heavy industrial development on reclaimed and remediated ground means substantial foundation, piling and slab work across many separate plots.

## The framework is the thing to understand

Civils are let through the **NEPO211 Civil and Infrastructure Works Framework**. A confirmed Lot 7 call-off went to Rainton Construction of Durham at **£11.79m**, running June 2025 to March 2026.

## The detail worth noticing

The Contracts Finder notice records that at expression-of-interest stage, **only two firms recorded interest** and were taken through to tender.

Two bidders on an eight-figure civils package. That says the regional civils market here is not crowded, which cuts both ways — fewer contractors to sell to, but each one carries more of the work and has less price pressure squeezing out anything that isn't strictly necessary.

## What to do

Understand the NEPO211 framework contractor list rather than chasing Teesworks. That list is the route to every plot.

## Sources

## Why it qualifies

Three 470MW reactors totalling 1.4GWe on one site — and **no construction contractor appointed**, with a final investment decision still ahead. The entire delivery structure is being assembled now.

## This is a fleet, not a project

Rolls-Royce SMR's whole proposition is **factory-built, standardised, repeatable** nuclear plants. Wylfa is the proving ground DESNZ expects to unlock fleet-scale deployment across other decommissioned sites.

Three identical units here, then more elsewhere, is repeatability at exactly the scale the model rewards most. A saving established once multiplies across the fleet.

## It connects directly to the East Midlands file

**Pioneer Works in Derby opens Q4 2026 specifically to establish the build processes, precision assembly and advanced testing that will be used at Wylfa.**

That is the same account, split across two regions. One conversation should cover both — and the East Midlands file separately flags an unresolved question about who is delivering SMR nuclear at Cottam, which may well be this programme again.

## The question that decides whether any of this is real

**Do concrete or precast elements feature materially in the SMR module design?**

Nothing published answers it. If the modules are mechanical and the concrete is conventional site-built containment, then the DfMA framing is wrong — this becomes a straightforward mass-concrete civils job instead. Still good, but a completely different pitch.

Settle that before anything else.

## Routing is genuinely ambiguous

Three pulls, deliberately left unset rather than picked silently:

- The site is UK shared patch
- DfMA and standardised modules point to **Avi**
- The fleet spans the UK, Czech Republic and Sweden, touching **Lisa's** Continental Europe patch

## Who is reachable now

No construction contractor, but plenty of named parties: GBE-N (Kenny Douglas), Rolls-Royce SMR, **Litmus Nuclear** (Amentum + Cavendish Nuclear, £300m owner's engineer over 14 years, covering construction assurance), and WSP/Mott MacDonald on permitting.

Litmus is the interesting one — an owner's engineer with a fourteen-year assurance remit across construction shapes what gets specified.

- NucNet, 4 March 2026; North Wales Live, February 2026

## Low — handed over

321 apartments, £38m, St Vincent Street. Handed over ahead of the 2026/27 academic year. Nothing to pour.

## Why it's recorded

Contractor intelligence. GRAHAM appears repeatedly across this sweep:

- **National Highways £1bn Legacy Concrete Roads Reconstruction framework** (2026-2032, with Kier and Sisk) — a framework literally named after the material
- Reported **sole bidder** to become strategic delivery partner on London Metropolitan University's £284m estate overhaul
- Southern Construction Framework London incumbent
- Active Scottish PBSA and education work, including a £10m Brunstane Primary retrofit

The Legacy Concrete Roads framework is the one that matters. Three contractors, £1bn, six years, and the whole thing is about reconstructing concrete carriageway.

That is worth more than any single Scottish PBSA.
